dx: Malignant pericardial effusion from metastatic lung adenocarcinoma
case: A 61-year-old woman who has never smoked comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of worsening shortness of breath, fatigue, and a dull sensation of fullness in her chest. Six months ago, biopsy of a right upper lobe lung mass showed adenocarcinoma. Pulse is 102/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 118/76 mm Hg. Physical examination shows distant heart sounds. Systolic pressure falls by 6 mm Hg with inspiration (normal fall is under 10 mm Hg). An ECG shows low QRS voltage, and a chest x-ray shows an enlarged, water-bottle-shaped cardiac silhouette. Echocardiography shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with no collapse of the right atrium or right ventricle. Pericardiocentesis drains 800 mL of bloody fluid. Diagnosis: malignant pericardial effusion from metastatic lung adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: Pericardiocentesis through the left fifth intercostal space immediately adjacent to the sternum is considered. Which of the following anatomic features allows a needle at this site to enter the pericardial sac without passing through the left lung?
options: The oblique fissure, which separates the left upper and lower lobes here
The costodiaphragmatic recess, which holds no lung during quiet breathing
The cardiac notch of the left lung, with a matching notch in the pleura
The lingula, which curls behind the heart and out of the needle path
approach: Picture what lies under the left fifth intercostal space beside the sternum.
Recall that the anterior border of the left lung and its pleura curve away from the midline at the level of the fourth and fifth costal cartilages.
That gap leaves part of the pericardium covered only by the chest wall, so a needle can enter the sac without crossing lung.
questions.why: The anterior border of the left lung bends laterally to form the cardiac notch, and the left pleural sac has a smaller notch in the same place. This leaves a small area of pericardium with no lung or pleura in front of it, sometimes called the bare area. A needle placed in the left fifth or sixth intercostal space close to the sternum can enter the pericardial sac here. Staying close to the sternum also matters because the internal thoracic artery runs just lateral to the sternal border.
whyNot: The oblique fissure is a cleft between two lobes. A needle placed into a fissure still passes through pleura and lung tissue on either side.
The costodiaphragmatic recess lies much lower, near the eighth to tenth ribs at the lateral chest wall, and it is still lined by parietal pleura. It is the target for draining a pleural effusion.
Correct.
The lingula is the tongue-shaped lower part of the left upper lobe. It lies in front of the heart, below the cardiac notch, so it would be in the way of a needle aimed lower.

topics: Surface anatomy of the lungs and pleura

questions.stem: Her 800-mL effusion developed without hypotension. In contrast, about 200 mL of blood accumulating within minutes after a penetrating cardiac wound can cause fatal tamponade. Which of the following properties of the pericardium best explains this difference?
options: The fibrous pericardium stretches when filled slowly, keeping sac pressure low
The serous pericardium absorbs slowly forming fluid as fast as it is produced
The right ventricle thickens over weeks and resists compression from outside
The pericardium stiffens over several weeks and shields the chambers from fluid
approach: Compare the two cases: a large volume tolerated versus a small volume that kills. The difference is the rate of filling.
Recall the pericardial pressure and volume curve: the tough fibrous pericardium is stiff over minutes but stretches over weeks.
Tamponade depends on the pressure inside the sac exceeding the filling pressures of the heart, and pressure is what slow filling keeps low.
questions.why: The fibrous pericardium is dense collagen that barely stretches over minutes. When fluid enters quickly, pressure in the sac rises steeply, exceeds right heart filling pressure, and the chambers cannot fill. When fluid builds over weeks, the sac gradually enlarges, so pressure rises little even with a large volume. This is why a slowly growing malignant effusion can reach 1 L or more before tamponade, while acute hemopericardium of about 200 mL can be fatal.
whyNot: Correct.
If the serous layer removed fluid as fast as it formed, no effusion would build up. Her 800 mL effusion shows that formation outpaced removal.
The right ventricle does not hypertrophy as a defense against outside pressure. Right ventricular hypertrophy follows pressure overload from inside, as in pulmonary hypertension.
A stiffer pericardium would raise sac pressure faster, making tamponade more likely. Stiffening and scarring describe constrictive pericarditis, which limits filling.

topics: Rate of fluid accumulation and tamponade

questions.stem: Molecular testing of her tumor shows a small deletion in one allele of the EGFR gene. The deletion keeps the receptor tyrosine kinase active in the absence of bound growth factor. Which of the following best describes this mutation?
options: Loss of function in a tumor suppressor gene, so both copies must be lost
Loss of function in a DNA mismatch repair gene, causing unstable repeats
Gain of function from a translocation that fuses two separate genes
Gain of function in a proto-oncogene, so one altered copy is enough
approach: Identify the effect: the receptor is active without its ligand, so the change adds function.
Classify the gene: a normal gene whose overactivity drives cell growth is a proto-oncogene.
Recall that activating changes in proto-oncogenes act dominantly at the cell level, so one altered allele is enough.
questions.why: EGFR is a receptor tyrosine kinase. Normally, binding of a growth factor causes the receptors to pair up and phosphorylate each other, which turns on growth signals such as the RAS and MAPK pathway. Small in-frame deletions in the kinase region keep the receptor active without ligand. Because the altered protein is overactive, one mutated copy drives growth even with a normal second copy. EGFR mutations are more common in lung adenocarcinomas of people who have never smoked.
whyNot: Tumor suppressors such as TP53 and RB1 usually need both copies lost (the two-hit model). Her mutation adds activity to a growth receptor, which is the opposite effect.
Mismatch repair defects, as in Lynch syndrome, cause microsatellite instability. They do not switch on a single receptor directly.
A fusion gene from a chromosomal rearrangement, such as EML4 and ALK in some lung adenocarcinomas, also adds function. Her change is a small deletion within one gene.
Correct.

questions.stem: Cytologic examination of the pericardial fluid shows clusters of large atypical cells, some forming small glands. Reactive mesothelial cells can have a similar appearance. Which of the following immunohistochemical staining patterns best supports metastatic lung adenocarcinoma?
options: Calretinin positive and TTF-1 negative
TTF-1 and napsin A positive, calretinin negative
CK20 and CDX2 positive, CK7 negative
S-100 and HMB-45 positive, pan-cytokeratin negative
approach: Name the two cell types to separate: reactive mesothelium versus metastatic lung adenocarcinoma.
Recall the markers: TTF-1 and napsin A mark lung adenocarcinoma, while calretinin marks mesothelial cells.
Pick the pattern that is positive for the lung markers and negative for the mesothelial marker.
questions.why: Lung and breast cancers are the most common sources of metastasis to the pericardium, and malignant effusions are often bloody. TTF-1 (thyroid transcription factor 1) and napsin A are expressed by most lung adenocarcinomas. Calretinin is a calcium-binding protein expressed by mesothelial cells and mesothelioma. A tumor cell population that is TTF-1 and napsin A positive and calretinin negative supports metastatic lung adenocarcinoma.
whyNot: This pattern marks mesothelial cells. It fits reactive mesothelium or mesothelioma.
Correct.
CK20 and CDX2 positive with CK7 negative is the typical colorectal adenocarcinoma pattern. Lung adenocarcinoma is usually CK7 positive and CK20 negative.
S-100 and HMB-45 positivity with no cytokeratin points to melanoma, which can also spread to the pericardium.

dx: Tuberculous pericardial effusion progressing to cardiac tamponade
case: A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV infection (CD4 count 140 cells/µL, reference 500 to 1500) is brought to the emergency department because of lightheadedness and shortness of breath for 2 days. He has had night sweats, weight loss, and cough for 6 weeks. Temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), pulse is 124/min, and blood pressure is 86/64 mm Hg. Physical examination shows jugular venous distention to the angle of the jaw and muffled heart sounds. Systolic pressure falls by 18 mm Hg with each inspiration (normal fall is under 10 mm Hg). Echocardiography shows a large pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right atrium and right ventricle. The drained fluid is an exudate with a high adenosine deaminase level, and culture later grows Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Diagnosis: tuberculous pericardial effusion progressing to cardiac tamponade.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best explains the large fall in his systolic pressure during each inspiration?
options: Inspiration raises intrathoracic pressure and squeezes the venae cavae shut
Inspiration triggers vagal slowing that lowers cardiac output with each breath
Inspiration lowers right ventricular filling, so less blood reaches the lungs
Inspiration adds right ventricular filling that bows the septum leftward
approach: Name the sign: a fall in systolic pressure of more than 10 mm Hg on inspiration is pulsus paradoxus.
Recall normal breathing effects: inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and increases venous return to the right heart.
Apply the fixed space: with the sac full, the right ventricle can only expand by pushing the septum into the left ventricle, which then fills less and ejects less.
questions.why: Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, which draws more blood into the right atrium and right ventricle. Normally the free walls of the heart expand to take this volume. In tamponade the fluid-filled sac fixes the total volume of the heart, so the extra right ventricular filling bows the interventricular septum toward the left ventricle. Left ventricular filling and stroke volume fall, so systolic pressure drops more than 10 mm Hg. This ventricular interdependence is the main cause of pulsus paradoxus.
whyNot: Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure. Raised intrathoracic pressure that limits venous return happens during a Valsalva maneuver or positive pressure ventilation.
Inspiration speeds the heart rate slightly by reducing vagal tone (respiratory sinus arrhythmia). Vagal slowing comes with expiration.
Inspiration increases right ventricular filling. The problem is that the extra right-sided volume crowds the left ventricle.
Correct.

questions.stem: Before the fluid is drained, a right heart catheter is placed. Normal values are right atrial (RA) pressure 2 to 6 mm Hg and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 6 to 12 mm Hg. Which of the following sets of pressures (mm Hg) is most likely to be found?
options: RA 2, RV 18/2, wedge 3
RA 5, RV 42/6, wedge 26
RA 17, RV 64/17, wedge 10
RA 19, RV 34/19, wedge 19
approach: Recall that in tamponade the pressure in the sac squeezes every chamber equally during diastole.
Predict that right atrial pressure, right ventricular diastolic pressure, and wedge pressure all rise to about the same value as the pericardial pressure.
Pick the set with high, equal diastolic pressures on both sides of the heart.
questions.why: In tamponade the chambers can only fill until their pressure matches the pressure in the pericardial sac. Because the fluid surrounds all four chambers, the diastolic pressures in the right atrium, right ventricle, and left atrium (measured as the wedge pressure) all rise and become nearly equal, often around 15 to 20 mm Hg. Equal, raised diastolic pressures across the heart are the classic catheter finding. Constrictive pericarditis also equalizes pressures, but the clinical picture of a large effusion and diastolic chamber collapse points to tamponade.
whyNot: Low pressures everywhere fit hypovolemia. His distended neck veins show that his right-sided pressure is high.
A high wedge pressure with a normal right atrial pressure points to left heart failure or mitral valve disease, with the left side congested and the right side spared.

A high right ventricular systolic pressure with a normal wedge pressure fits pulmonary hypertension or a pulmonary embolus with right heart strain. The left-sided filling pressure is not raised to match.
Correct.

questions.stem: A pericardial biopsy specimen shows caseating granulomas. Which of the following cytokines, secreted by CD4+ T lymphocytes, activates his macrophages to kill this organism and form granulomas?
options: Interferon gamma
Interleukin 4
Interleukin 12
Transforming growth factor beta
approach: Recognize the response: granulomas are a cell-mediated (type IV) response to an intracellular organism.
Identify the helper cell: Th1 CD4 T cells drive this response.
Name the Th1 cytokine that activates macrophages: interferon gamma.
questions.why: Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside macrophages. Macrophages present its antigens and release interleukin 12, which pushes CD4 T cells toward the Th1 type. Th1 cells release interferon gamma, which activates macrophages to kill ingested bacilli and to transform into epithelioid cells and giant cells that form granulomas. With few CD4 cells, people with HIV form poor granulomas and are prone to spread of tuberculosis outside the lungs, including to the pericardium.
whyNot: Correct.
Interleukin 4 comes from Th2 cells. It drives IgE class switching and allergic responses and does not activate macrophages to kill mycobacteria.
Interleukin 12 is made by macrophages and dendritic cells. It steers T cells toward Th1, but it comes from the macrophage side of the loop.
Transforming growth factor beta comes from regulatory T cells and other cells. It dampens immune responses and promotes fibrosis.

questions.stem: The organism stains poorly with Gram stain but retains carbol fuchsin after decolorization with acid-alcohol. Which of the following components of its cell envelope is responsible for this staining property?
options: Lipoteichoic acid
Lipopolysaccharide
Mycolic acid
Polysaccharide capsule
approach: Name the stain: holding carbol fuchsin after an acid-alcohol wash means the organism is acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen stain).
Recall what makes mycobacteria acid-fast: a waxy, lipid-rich cell wall.
Pick the long-chain fatty acid that forms that waxy layer.
questions.why: Mycobacteria have a cell wall rich in mycolic acids, very long-chain fatty acids linked to arabinogalactan and peptidoglycan. This waxy layer keeps out the crystal violet and iodine of the Gram stain, so the organism stains poorly. Once carbol fuchsin is driven in with heat, the same layer holds the dye against acid-alcohol, which is what acid-fast means. Mycolic acids also help the organism resist drying and survive inside macrophages.
whyNot: Lipoteichoic acid is found in Gram-positive cell walls. It anchors the wall to the membrane and triggers inflammation, and it does not make cells acid-fast.
Lipopolysaccharide is the endotoxin of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria. Mycobacteria lack it.
Correct.
A polysaccharide capsule, as in Streptococcus pneumoniae, blocks phagocytosis. Capsules are shown with special stains and do not cause acid-fastness.

case: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because of sharp central chest pain for 2 days. The pain worsens when he lies supine or inspires deeply, improves when he sits up and leans forward, and radiates to the ridge of the left trapezius muscle. One week ago he had a sore throat, fever, and diarrhea, and his roommate had a similar illness. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F). Auscultation with the patient leaning forward shows a scratchy, three-component sound at the left sternal border. An ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR depression. Serum troponin is within the reference range. Echocardiography shows a small pericardial effusion with normal wall motion. Stool PCR detects coxsackievirus B. Diagnosis: acute viral pericarditis.

questions.stem: Pain from his inflamed parietal pericardium is referred to the skin over the trapezius ridge. Which of the following nerves carries this pain?
options: Vagus nerve, through its cardiac branches
Phrenic nerve, from spinal segments C3 to C5
Upper thoracic sympathetic afferents, from T1 to T4
Intercostobrachial nerve, from spinal segment T2
approach: Identify the pain source: the parietal pericardium, which has sensory fibers, unlike the visceral layer.
Recall its nerve supply: the phrenic nerve, which runs between the fibrous pericardium and the mediastinal pleura.
Link segments to skin: C3 to C5 also supply the skin over the trapezius ridge and shoulder, so the brain maps the pain there.
questions.why: The fibrous pericardium and the parietal layer of serous pericardium receive sensory fibers from the phrenic nerves, which arise from C3 to C5. The skin over the trapezius ridge is supplied by the same cervical segments through the supraclavicular nerves. Pain from the parietal pericardium is therefore referred to that area. Trapezius ridge pain is a useful clue that separates pericarditis from myocardial ischemia.
whyNot: The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to the heart and visceral sensations such as stretch, which take part in reflexes. It does not carry the pain of pericarditis.
Correct.
Sympathetic afferents from T1 to T4 carry pain from the heart muscle itself. That explains ischemic pain referred to the chest wall and medial left arm.
The intercostobrachial nerve supplies skin of the axilla and medial upper arm. It carries no fibers from the pericardium.

questions.stem: His ECG shows ST-segment elevation in most leads, reflecting an injury current in the outer myocardium. Which of the following features of the heart wall best explains how pericardial inflammation affects the myocardium?
options: The fibrous pericardium is fused to the myocardium with no space between them
The endocardium continues around the valve rings onto the outer heart surface
The parietal serous layer is attached directly to the outer myocardium
The epicardium is the visceral serous layer and lies on the myocardium
approach: List the layers from outside in: fibrous pericardium, parietal serous layer, pericardial cavity, visceral serous layer (epicardium), myocardium, endocardium.
Notice which inflamed layer touches heart muscle: the visceral serous layer is the epicardium itself.
Conclude that inflammation of the epicardium spreads to the subepicardial myocardium, producing diffuse ST elevation.
questions.why: The serous pericardium has two layers. The parietal layer lines the inside of the fibrous pericardium, and the visceral layer covers the heart as the epicardium. The epicardium is a layer of mesothelium over loose connective tissue and fat that carries the coronary vessels, and it sits directly on the myocardium. Inflammation of the epicardium irritates the outer myocardium beneath it. Because the whole surface is involved, ST elevation appears in most leads, not in one coronary territory.
whyNot: The fibrous pericardium is the outer sac. It is separated from the heart by the two serous layers and the pericardial cavity.
The endocardium lines the inside of the chambers and covers the valves. It does not wrap onto the outer surface of the heart.
The parietal serous layer lines the fibrous pericardium. It faces the heart across the pericardial cavity and does not touch the myocardium.
Correct.

questions.stem: Purified RNA from this virus, without any viral proteins, can initiate infection when introduced into a cell. Which of the following features of the virus best explains this finding?
options: Negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome packaged with its own polymerase
Double-stranded RNA genome split into segments within a nonenveloped capsid
Positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome that serves directly as mRNA
RNA genome that is copied into DNA by a reverse transcriptase it carries
approach: Identify the virus: coxsackievirus B is an enterovirus in the picornavirus family.
Recall its genome: nonenveloped, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA.
Reason it out: host ribosomes can translate a positive-sense genome right away, making the viral polymerase, so naked RNA is infectious.
questions.why: Picornaviruses such as coxsackievirus have a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome. It reads like mRNA, so host ribosomes translate it into one large polyprotein that is cut into viral proteins, including the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Because the virus needs nothing from the virion to start, the purified RNA alone is infectious. Coxsackievirus B spreads by the fecal-oral route and is a leading cause of viral pericarditis and myocarditis.
whyNot: Negative-sense RNA must first be copied into positive-sense mRNA by the polymerase carried in the virion, so the naked RNA alone cannot start infection. Influenza and measles viruses work this way.
Double-stranded RNA viruses such as rotavirus must bring their own polymerase to make mRNA, so their naked genome is not infectious.
Correct.
Retroviruses such as HIV need the reverse transcriptase packaged in the virion to make DNA, so their purified RNA alone does not start infection.

questions.stem: The scratchy, three-component sound at his left sternal border is a pericardial friction rub. Which of the following types of exudate on the pericardial surfaces is most likely responsible for this sound?
options: Fibrinous exudate that roughens the serous surfaces
Serous fluid with few cells that pools between the layers
Purulent exudate packed with neutrophils and bacteria
Caseous material from necrotizing granulomas
approach: Recall the usual pattern of viral pericarditis: fibrinous or serofibrinous inflammation.
Link the pattern to the sound: deposits of fibrin make the smooth serous surfaces rough.
Rough layers rubbing together with each heartbeat produce the scratchy rub.
questions.why: Acute viral pericarditis usually produces a fibrinous or serofibrinous exudate. Fibrin deposits make the normally smooth, moist serous layers dry and shaggy, sometimes called bread and butter pericarditis. As the heart moves, these rough surfaces rub, producing a scratchy sound that can have three parts linked to atrial systole, ventricular systole, and early ventricular filling. The same fibrinous pattern is seen in pericarditis after a myocardial infarction and in uremia.
whyNot: Correct.
Thin serous fluid separates the layers and keeps them smooth. A large serous effusion tends to muffle heart sounds and can make a rub fade.
Purulent pericarditis follows bacterial spread, for example from pneumonia or a chest wound. It fits a very ill patient with high fever, and his course and virus test point to a viral cause.
Caseous pericarditis comes from tuberculosis or fungal infection and develops over weeks. His acute illness after a viral prodrome does not fit.

dx: Bicuspid aortic valve with coarctation of the aorta in Turner syndrome
case: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of short stature and absent breast development. Her height is 142 cm. Physical examination shows a broad chest with widely spaced nipples and a low posterior hairline. Blood pressure is 152/88 mm Hg in the right arm and 104/70 mm Hg in the right leg (normally the leg pressure equals or exceeds the arm pressure). Femoral pulses are weak and delayed. Auscultation shows an ejection click and a soft midsystolic murmur at the right upper sternal border and a separate systolic murmur over the left upper back. Karyotype is 45,X. Echocardiography shows a bicuspid aortic valve with mild stenosis, a mildly dilated ascending aorta, and coarctation of the aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery. Diagnosis: bicuspid aortic valve with coarctation of the aorta in Turner syndrome.

questions.stem: In a 46,XX female, most genes on one X chromosome are inactivated in each cell. Which of the following best explains why loss of the second X chromosome causes this patient's short stature?
options: Some X genes, such as SHOX, escape inactivation and need two working copies
Her remaining X carries an expanded trinucleotide repeat that silences growth genes
Her single X is always paternal, and imprinting silences its growth genes
Her cells inactivate the single remaining X, so no X genes are expressed
approach: Note the puzzle: if one X is normally silenced, a female with one X should match a 46,XX female.
Resolve it: some X genes escape inactivation, including those in the pseudoautosomal region shared with Y, so normal cells use two active copies.
Apply it: with one X, these genes are expressed at half dose. Half a dose of SHOX causes short stature.
questions.why: X inactivation silences most of one X chromosome in each female cell, but a set of genes escapes it. These include genes in the pseudoautosomal regions, which are shared with the Y chromosome so that males also carry two copies. SHOX lies in pseudoautosomal region 1 and is needed in two copies for normal long bone growth. A 45,X female has only one copy, and this haploinsufficiency explains much of the short stature in Turner syndrome. Loss of other escaping genes is thought to contribute to the other features.
whyNot: Correct.
Trinucleotide repeat expansion causes disorders such as fragile X syndrome and Huntington disease. Turner syndrome is a loss of a whole chromosome.
In most cases of Turner syndrome the single X comes from the mother, because the paternal sex chromosome is the one lost. Imprinting does not explain the short stature.
A cell with one X keeps it active. X inactivation leaves one active X in every cell, and a cell with no active X could not survive.

topics: X inactivation and genes that escape it

questions.stem: A chest x-ray shows notching of the inferior borders of several posterior ribs, caused by enlarged collateral arteries that bypass the narrowed segment. Which of the following collateral pathways is responsible for the rib notching?
options: Superior epigastric arteries to the inferior epigastric arteries
Vertebral arteries joining to form the basilar artery
Internal thoracic arteries to the intercostal arteries
Celiac trunk to the superior mesenteric artery through pancreatic arcades
approach: Locate the block: the coarctation lies just distal to the left subclavian artery, so the subclavian arteries are proximal to it and the descending aorta is distal.
Find a bridge: the internal thoracic artery (a subclavian branch) feeds anterior intercostal arteries, which connect to posterior intercostal arteries from the descending aorta.
Link to the x-ray: the enlarged, tortuous posterior intercostal arteries run in the costal grooves and erode the lower rib borders.
questions.why: With coarctation distal to the left subclavian artery, blood reaches the lower body by detouring around the narrowing. The internal thoracic arteries arise from the subclavian arteries and give off anterior intercostal arteries. These connect with the posterior intercostal arteries, which carry blood backward into the descending aorta beyond the coarctation. The posterior intercostal arteries enlarge and press on the costal grooves on the lower edge of the ribs, producing notching. The first two ribs are usually spared because their intercostal arteries come from the costocervical trunk.
whyNot: The internal thoracic artery also continues as the superior epigastric artery, which joins the inferior epigastric artery in the rectus sheath. This collateral carries blood to the lower body but runs in the abdominal wall, so it does not notch ribs.
The vertebral arteries arise from the subclavian arteries proximal to the coarctation and supply the brain. Their junction as the basilar artery is normal anatomy and does not bypass the aorta.
Correct.
Pancreaticoduodenal arcades connect the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery. They enlarge with narrowing of one of those vessels and lie in the abdomen.

topics: Collateral circulation in coarctation of the aorta

questions.stem: If her aortic stenosis worsens over the years, her left ventricle will face a higher systolic pressure, and its wall will thicken while the chamber size stays normal. Which of the following relationships best explains why this thickening benefits the ventricle?
options: Frank-Starling law: more stretch of the fibers raises the force of contraction
Law of Laplace: wall stress rises with pressure and radius, falls with thickness
Poiseuille law: resistance to flow rises steeply as the radius of a tube falls
Fick principle: flow equals oxygen uptake divided by arteriovenous O2 difference
approach: Identify the load: aortic stenosis causes pressure overload of the left ventricle.
Recall the law that links pressure, chamber size, and wall thickness: Laplace, wall stress equals pressure times radius divided by twice the wall thickness.
Apply it: a thicker wall brings stress back toward normal, which is why pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy.
questions.why: By the law of Laplace, wall stress is about pressure times radius divided by twice the wall thickness. When systolic pressure rises, as with aortic stenosis or coarctation, stress on the wall rises. Adding sarcomeres in parallel thickens the wall and brings stress back toward normal without enlarging the chamber, a pattern called concentric hypertrophy. The cost is a stiffer ventricle with impaired filling and a higher oxygen demand.
whyNot: The Frank-Starling law links end-diastolic volume to stroke volume. It explains beat-to-beat matching of output to filling and does not explain why a thicker wall lowers stress.
Correct.
Poiseuille law explains why a narrow valve or vessel greatly increases resistance to flow. It explains why the stenosis raises pressure, but it does not explain the response of the ventricular wall.
The Fick principle is used to measure cardiac output or organ blood flow from oxygen uptake. It says nothing about wall stress.

questions.stem: A dilated ascending aorta is common with a bicuspid aortic valve and increases the later risk of aneurysm and dissection. The main abnormality lies in the layer that normally gives the aorta its elastic recoil. Which of the following is most likely to be seen on histologic examination of this layer?
options: Lipid-filled foam cells under a fibrous cap in the intima
Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum in the adventitia
Granulomas with giant cells surrounding a fragmented elastic lamina
Fragmented elastic lamellae and loss of smooth muscle in the media
approach: Recall the structure of an elastic artery: the media of the aorta holds many layers of elastic lamellae with smooth muscle between them.
Identify the lesion of bicuspid valve aortopathy: noninflammatory medial degeneration.
Pick the option that describes loss of elastic tissue and smooth muscle in the media with no inflammation.
questions.why: The aorta is an elastic artery. Its thick media contains dozens of concentric elastic lamellae with smooth muscle cells and matrix between them, which let it stretch in systole and recoil in diastole. In aortas linked to a bicuspid valve, as in Marfan syndrome, the media shows medial degeneration: elastic lamellae fragment, smooth muscle cells are lost, and pools of proteoglycan-rich matrix collect. The weakened wall dilates and can tear, causing dissection.
whyNot: Foam cells and a fibrous cap in the intima describe an atherosclerotic plaque. Atherosclerosis mainly affects the abdominal aorta and is the main cause of abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum is the lesion of tertiary syphilis. It starves the media of blood and gives a tree-bark appearance to the aortic root.
Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells near the internal elastic lamina describes giant cell arteritis or Takayasu arteritis. Her aortic dilation has no inflammation.
Correct.

dx: Patent ductus arteriosus with congenital rubella syndrome
case: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of poor feeding, sweating during feeds, and poor weight gain. Her mother was never vaccinated and had a fever and a fine rash during the first trimester. The infant has bilateral cataracts and failed her newborn hearing screen. Pulse is 168/min (normal about 100 to 160), and blood pressure is 82/34 mm Hg, a wide pulse pressure for her age. Peripheral pulses are bounding. A continuous, machine-like murmur is heard best below the left clavicle. Echocardiography shows a large patent ductus arteriosus with left-to-right flow and an enlarged left atrium and left ventricle. Diagnosis: patent ductus arteriosus with congenital rubella syndrome.

questions.stem: Serologic testing for rubella is performed. Which of the following results best indicates that the infant was infected in utero rather than carrying antibody passed from her mother?
options: Rubella IgG in her serum at the same level as her mother's
Rubella IgA in her mother's breast milk
Rubella-specific IgM in her own serum
Rubella IgG in her serum that falls steadily over her first 6 months
approach: Recall which antibody class crosses the placenta: only IgG, through neonatal Fc receptors.
Reason that any IgM in the infant must have been made by the infant herself.
Conclude that rubella-specific IgM in her serum shows her own immune response to infection.
questions.why: IgG is the only antibody class carried across the placenta, so every newborn whose mother is immune has maternal rubella IgG. IgM is a large pentamer that does not cross. Rubella-specific IgM in an infant's serum therefore means the infant's own B cells responded to the virus, which confirms congenital infection. Rubella IgG that persists beyond the age when maternal IgG should have disappeared, roughly 6 to 12 months, also supports the diagnosis.
whyNot: IgG equal to the mother's level is what passive placental transfer produces. It cannot separate infection from maternal antibody.
IgA in breast milk is made by the mother and protects the infant's gut. It says nothing about whether the infant was infected.
Correct.
A steady fall in IgG over the first months is the expected decay of maternal antibody (half-life about 3 to 4 weeks). It points away from the infant making her own antibody.

questions.stem: During surgical ligation of the ductus, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which curves under the aortic arch beside the ductus, is at risk. The ductus and the low course of this nerve on the left are both explained by the same pharyngeal arch artery. Which of the following arch arteries is it?
options: Left sixth arch artery
Left fourth arch artery
Left third arch artery
Left second arch artery
approach: Recall the derivatives: the sixth arch arteries form the proximal pulmonary arteries, and the distal part of the left sixth forms the ductus arteriosus.
Recall that the recurrent laryngeal nerves are sixth arch nerves that hook under the sixth arch arteries as the heart descends.
On the left the distal sixth artery persists as the ductus, so the nerve stays hooked under it beside the aortic arch.
questions.why: The recurrent laryngeal nerves supply the muscles of the sixth pharyngeal arch and loop beneath the sixth arch arteries. On the right, the distal sixth arch artery and the fifth disappear, so the right nerve moves up and hooks around the right subclavian artery, a fourth arch derivative. On the left, the distal sixth arch artery persists as the ductus arteriosus, which becomes the ligamentum arteriosum. The left nerve therefore stays hooked under the aortic arch next to the ductus, where it can be injured in ductus surgery.
whyNot: Correct.
The left fourth arch artery forms part of the aortic arch. The left nerve passes under the arch, but its low course is set by the sixth arch artery, the ductus.
The third arch arteries form the common carotid arteries and the start of the internal carotid arteries. They are unrelated to the ductus.
The second arch artery mostly regresses and leaves small remnants such as the stapedial artery. It does not form the ductus.

topics: Course of the recurrent laryngeal nerves

questions.stem: Before birth, patency of the ductus is maintained by prostaglandin E2, produced by both the placenta and the ductus wall. Which of the following precursors and enzymes produce prostaglandin E2?
options: Arachidonic acid, by 5-lipoxygenase
Sphingosine, by sphingosine kinase
Cholesterol, by side-chain cleavage enzyme
Arachidonic acid, by cyclooxygenase
approach: Classify the molecule: prostaglandins are eicosanoids, 20-carbon signals made from a membrane fatty acid.
Name the precursor: arachidonic acid, released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2.
Split the pathways: cyclooxygenase makes prostaglandins and thromboxanes, while 5-lipoxygenase makes leukotrienes.
questions.why: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid, a 20-carbon omega-6 fatty acid, from membrane phospholipids. Cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2) turns it into prostaglandin H2, which other enzymes convert to prostaglandin E2, prostacyclin, and thromboxane A2. PGE2 relaxes the smooth muscle of the ductus. After birth the placental source is gone and the lungs break down circulating PGE2, so the level falls and the ductus constricts. This is why COX inhibitors can close a patent ductus and why PGE1 is given to keep it open in duct-dependent heart defects.
whyNot: 5-lipoxygenase turns arachidonic acid into leukotrienes, which cause bronchoconstriction and attract neutrophils. It does not make prostaglandins.
Sphingosine kinase makes sphingosine 1-phosphate, a lipid signal that guides lymphocyte movement. It is unrelated to prostaglandin synthesis.
Side-chain cleavage of cholesterol is the first step in steroid hormone synthesis. Prostaglandins are made from a fatty acid.
Correct.

questions.stem: Suppose her ductus is never closed. Years later, pulmonary vascular resistance rises until flow through the ductus reverses (Eisenmenger syndrome). Her toes become cyanotic and clubbed while her fingers remain pink. Which of the following anatomic facts best explains this pattern?
options: The ductus joins the aorta at its root, before the coronary arteries arise
The ductus joins the aorta just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery
The ductus joins the arch between the brachiocephalic trunk and the left common carotid
The ductus joins the right subclavian artery close to where that vessel begins
approach: Identify the shunt: with reversed flow, deoxygenated blood moves from the pulmonary artery into the aorta through the ductus.
Locate where it enters: the ductus joins the aorta just beyond the origin of the left subclavian artery.
Trace the distribution: branches that leave the aorta before that point (to the head and arms) carry oxygenated blood, while the descending aorta carries mixed blood to the lower body.
questions.why: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk near its bifurcation to the aorta just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery. When pulmonary pressure exceeds aortic pressure, deoxygenated blood enters the aorta at this point. The brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian arteries have already branched off and still carry well-oxygenated blood to the head and arms. The descending aorta carries the mixed blood to the legs, so cyanosis and clubbing appear in the toes but not the fingers (differential cyanosis).
whyNot: Entry at the aortic root would send deoxygenated blood to every branch, including the coronary arteries, causing cyanosis of both hands and feet.
Correct.
Entry between the brachiocephalic trunk and the left common carotid would also darken the left head and arm. The ductus enters further along, past all three arch branches.
The ductus does not connect to the right subclavian artery. If it did, the right arm would turn blue.

dx: Ostium secundum atrial septal defect in Holt-Oram syndrome
case: A 29-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of shortness of breath when climbing stairs and recent episodes of palpitations. Her father and brother have similar thumb abnormalities, and her father had a congenital heart defect repaired as a child. Physical examination shows bilateral hypoplastic thumbs. The second heart sound is widely split and does not vary with respiration. A soft midsystolic murmur is heard at the left upper sternal border. An ECG shows incomplete right bundle branch block. Echocardiography shows a 14-mm defect in the center of the atrial septum at the fossa ovalis with left-to-right flow, an enlarged right atrium and right ventricle, and a pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio (Qp:Qs) of 2.1 (normal 1.0). Genetic testing shows a TBX5 mutation. Diagnosis: ostium secundum atrial septal defect in Holt-Oram syndrome.

questions.stem: She asks about the risk to her future children. Based on her family history, which of the following is the inheritance pattern of her condition and the risk to each child?
options: Autosomal recessive, 25% for each child
X-linked dominant, 50% for each child
Mitochondrial, nearly 100% for each child
Autosomal dominant, 50% for each child
approach: Read the pedigree: affected people appear in two generations, and her father passed it to a son (her brother).
Rule out patterns: father-to-son transmission excludes X-linked inheritance, and a father cannot pass on mitochondrial DNA.
Conclude autosomal dominant: an affected parent passes the mutant allele to each child with a 50% chance.
questions.why: Holt-Oram syndrome is autosomal dominant and is caused by mutations in TBX5, a transcription factor needed for development of the upper limb and the heart. Her family shows affected people in each generation and transmission from father to son, which fits autosomal dominant inheritance. Each child of an affected parent has a 50% chance of inheriting the mutant allele. Severity can vary within a family, so an affected child may have different heart or limb findings from hers.
whyNot: Autosomal recessive traits usually appear in siblings of unaffected carrier parents, not in parent and child across generations. Her child would be at risk only if her partner were also a carrier.
A father passes his X chromosome only to daughters, so father-to-son transmission rules out any X-linked pattern.
Mitochondria are passed down through the egg, so an affected father cannot pass on a mitochondrial disorder.
Correct.

questions.stem: A secundum defect forms when the flap that should cover the foramen ovale is too short, often from excessive resorption. Which of the following embryonic structures normally forms this flap, the floor of the fossa ovalis?
options: Septum secundum
Septum primum
Endocardial cushions
Sinus venosus
approach: Recall the two atrial septa: the thin septum primum grows first, and the thick septum secundum grows to its right.
Recall the opening: the foramen ovale is a gap in the septum secundum that the septum primum covers from the left like a flap valve.
Link to the adult heart: the septum primum becomes the floor of the fossa ovalis, and the septum secundum forms its rim (limbus).
questions.why: The septum primum grows down toward the endocardial cushions. Before it fuses, holes appear in its upper part and merge into the ostium secundum. The thicker septum secundum then grows on its right side but leaves an opening, the foramen ovale. The septum primum acts as a flap valve over this opening, letting blood pass from right to left in the fetus. After birth, rising left atrial pressure presses the flap against the septum secundum, and it becomes the floor of the fossa ovalis. If the septum primum is resorbed too much, the flap is too short and a secundum defect remains.
whyNot: The septum secundum forms the thick upper rim (limbus) of the fossa ovalis. A small septum secundum can also cause a secundum defect, but it is not the flap.
Correct.

The endocardial cushions close the ostium primum and form part of the atrioventricular valves. Failure here causes an ostium primum defect or an atrioventricular septal defect, often in Down syndrome.
The sinus venosus forms the smooth part of the right atrium. A defect near the opening of the superior vena cava is a sinus venosus defect, which lies outside the fossa ovalis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her second heart sound is widely split and does not vary with respiration?
options: Shunt flow keeps right ventricular volume about equal in both breathing phases
Delayed left ventricular activation makes the aortic valve close after the pulmonic valve
High pulmonary artery pressure makes the pulmonic valve close early with every beat
Right bundle branch block delays right ventricular contraction only on inspiration
approach: Recall normal splitting: inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, delaying pulmonic valve closure, so the split widens.
Add the defect: the large left-to-right shunt keeps the right ventricle loaded, so pulmonic closure is late in every beat.
Explain the fixed part: when inspiration brings more systemic venous blood to the right atrium, less blood crosses from the left atrium, so right ventricular volume barely changes.
questions.why: In an atrial septal defect the two atria act as one shared chamber. Shunted blood adds to right ventricular volume, prolonging right ventricular ejection and delaying pulmonic valve closure, so S2 is widely split. During inspiration, more systemic venous blood returns to the right atrium, but this raises right atrial pressure slightly and reduces the left-to-right flow across the defect. During expiration the shunt increases again. Right ventricular filling stays about the same through the breathing cycle, so the split is fixed.
whyNot: Correct.
Delayed left ventricular activation, as in left bundle branch block, delays aortic closure and causes paradoxical splitting, which narrows on inspiration.
High pulmonary artery pressure makes P2 loud. It does not explain a split that stays wide and fixed, and her shunt flow is still left to right.
Right bundle branch block widens the split, but the split still increases on inspiration because the breathing effect on venous return remains. Block affects every beat, not only inspiration.

questions.stem: Before her defect is closed, she develops a deep vein thrombosis of the calf. Immediately after straining to lift a heavy box, she has sudden weakness of the right face and arm from an embolic stroke. Which of the following events best explains how a venous thrombus reached her brain?
options: Left atrial pressure briefly rose above right atrial pressure
Pulmonary capillaries widened enough for the clot to pass through
Right atrial pressure briefly rose above left atrial pressure
The clot crossed from the pulmonary artery to the aorta by a ductus
approach: Name the event: a venous clot causing a stroke is a paradoxical embolism, which needs a path from the right heart to the left heart.
Recall the usual direction: left atrial pressure is normally higher, so her shunt runs left to right.
Apply the trigger: straining, then releasing it, sends a surge of venous blood to the right atrium, so right atrial pressure briefly exceeds left atrial pressure and the clot crosses the defect.
questions.why: Normally left atrial pressure is a few mm Hg higher than right atrial pressure, so flow across an atrial septal defect is left to right. Straining against a closed glottis (a Valsalva maneuver) holds back venous return, and when the strain is released, pooled venous blood rushes into the right atrium. For a few beats right atrial pressure exceeds left atrial pressure, and blood, along with any clot it carries, crosses into the left atrium and the systemic arteries. Coughing can have the same effect. This is a paradoxical embolism.
whyNot: Left atrial pressure higher than right atrial pressure is the usual state and drives left-to-right flow. It would carry blood away from the systemic side, not bring a venous clot to it.
Pulmonary capillaries are about 5 to 10 µm wide and trap venous clots, which is how pulmonary emboli form. They do not widen enough to let a clot through.
Correct.
Her echocardiogram shows an atrial septal defect only. A ductus is a different shunt, and she has no evidence of one.
